# Redline run judge brief

You judge one run of a reviewing Skill. The Skill received one text, `work/input.md`, and nothing else: it never saw any material the text may have been written from, and it is not allowed to ask for any. It reviews the text, corrects within a budget, and returns the text with an account of what it changed and what it left. Its reply is `response.md`, and the text it delivered, where it delivered one, is `delivered.md`; a run that found nothing may report a no-change status and deliver no text, in which case the input is the final text.

Read `work/input.md`, `response.md`, `delivered.md` where present, and criteria.md; read nothing else. No source package is staged here. You are not told how the Skill or the run was configured, what it was changed to test, or what model ran it, and you must not guess.

## Criterion R1

Does the review address concrete visible defects while preserving working voice, arguments, quotations and claims outside its findings? Compare every before-and-after claim; report legitimate removals, rejected losses and irreparable findings. A clean text is not rewritten to satisfy taste. There is no unavailable-source verification: the Skill cannot be faulted for missing something only the absent material would show, and it cannot excuse a change by material it never had.

## What to write

Write one Markdown file at the path you are given, in the run directory:

1. **Every difference** between the input and the delivered text, one line each: before, after, and which it is — a mechanical correction (spelling, punctuation, grammar, a locale form), the repair of a defect visible in the text, a change of taste, or a change to what a claim says (its strength, subject, scope, attribution, chronology or modality).
2. **Bridges into quotations.** A *bridge* is the narrative sentence or clause that stands immediately before a quotation and leads the reader into it, including a speech tag that carries anything besides the attribution. Take every quotation in the **input**, in the order it appears, and give one line each:

   - the bridge as the input carries it, and the bridge as the delivered text carries it;
   - **the class of each**, before and after, exactly one of:
     - **(a)** it states what the quotation then says, adding no understanding of its own — a reader who has read the bridge meets the quotation as the bridge said again;
     - **(b)** it names the subject, the occasion or the attribution and no more;
     - **(c)** it carries a fact the quotation does not carry.

     Choose one class for each side and give the words that put it there. Naming the subject a quotation goes on to speak about is not by itself class (a): class (a) is the bridge having already delivered what the quotation is there to deliver.
   - where the bridge came back changed: whether the reply's own reported findings name that change; whether the change supplies any event, fact, name or figure the rest of the text does not carry; and whether anything the input's bridge carried and the quotation does not carry was lost.
3. **Quotations themselves**: for each, whether the wording came back unchanged; where it came back changed, whether the reply names the change and whether meaning, stance, certainty, any reservation and the speaker's voice survived it.
4. **G1, G2, P1, W1, L1, L2, R1**: pass, fail or skipped individually, using criteria.md. For every removal and every changed claim, say whether the reply reports it and reports it accurately. R1: pass or fail. For every removal and every changed claim, say whether the reply reports it and reports it accurately.

Give a complete judgement with all requested sections. Save it as judgement.md and include it in your final response. Do not inspect traces or model identities. Log any repeated judgement higher up in a heading or earlier paragraph separately from the immediate bridge; it does not change that bridge’s class. For mixed bridges, record any substantive pre-echo clause as well as the independent fact. Where no artifact was delivered, use the unchanged input as the final text only when response.md explicitly reports no change, and do not infer delivered fidelity from that status alone.

Reviewed as a case study in British English (`en_GB`), with no technique, as specified in the metadata.

```markdown
  genre: casestudy
  technique: none
  language: en_GB

# Fenwick staff could see which instruments awaited parts

Fenwick Instrument Repairs’ trial summary records 38 jobs entered in a shared bench schedule. The manager approved continued use for new jobs, while the backlog awaited a review of status definitions.

By Thomas Barregren

Jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets at Fenwick Instrument Repairs, which services brass and woodwind instruments. In January 2026, the team began a six-week trial with Benchline after checking that it could distinguish those statuses.

## Benchline configures the workshop’s choices

The team defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers.

Asked in an email interview on 2 March 2026 what the team had to settle, manager Priya Vale wrote: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary does not measure repair duration

The trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule and says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

Vale approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.

## Vale reflects on the next steps

Asked about making the same choice again and what would change, Vale wrote: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’
```

# Semantic criteria

| ID | Question and evidence | Applies |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | Does every assertion, quotation, attribution and implication stay within the supplied material, including uncertainty, chronology, causal limits and author perspective? Cite any unsupported addition or dropped caveat. Count-size judgements need a supplied comparison. | Write, source-aware evaluator only |
| G1 | Does the chosen genre do its job for the named reader, keep a recognisable angle and carry the appropriate journalistic or copy/UX craft? Cite what the reader learns, sees, considers or can do. | Both |
| G2 | Do the required parts perform distinct useful jobs? Each of the four article genres carries the anatomy's parts in its order — headline, standfirst, byline, lead, sections, an ending that calls the reader to action — and each part does its own job: a headline and subheadings that state the angle of what they head and are understood on their own without claiming more than the text claims or repeating the standfirst or the first sentence under them, a standfirst that stands alone, a lead that begins the work and comes before the first H2, an explanatory body, an ending that shows the lead's expectation met. The byline names the author the brief names, or the invoking user where the brief names none, which a Write run states in its delivery account; a Redline run on a text whose author nobody names reports the byline as missing and leaves it unfilled. Article: explanatory body, and a call to action that is the useful next step the explanation supports, commercial only where the assignment warrants. Case: customer situation/action/results/appraisal, truthful publisher stance, and a call to action built from supplied offers, links or contact routes. Column: personal reflection, not compulsory anecdote or campaign, and a call to action that grows out of the reflection and may stand beside honest uncertainty. Opinion: early position, support, relevant real objection, and the change or stance as the call to action, with an identifiable actor. Web-copy: useful information/choice, conditions and accurate next-step consequence where applicable. | Both; excerpt control exempts full article form |
| P1 | Can this reader follow the reasoning, with unfamiliar concepts introduced before use, real transitions and conclusions proportionate to visible support? Does useful technical substance remain? | Both; Redline uses text alone |
| W1 | Can a web reader orient and enter the text without losing its continuous explanation or voice? Are paragraphs coherent with useful rhythm, headings informative where the genre needs them, and standfirst and lead complementary — the body complete when the standfirst is covered, and the two opening on different first words? Identify actual reader loss for density or fragmentation. In the four article genres a requirement is judged by counting; a departure from a *should* — a paragraph over 80 words, a section over three paragraphs, a heading level below the second, a headline past eight words or 60 characters, a standfirst and a lead opening on the same first word — is a failure only where following the norm was possible and the text is no better for having left it; *most* — two or three sentences to a paragraph, two or three paragraphs to a section — is read across the whole text and never against one paragraph or one section. For `webcopy` the scale stays advisory. | Both |
| L1 | Does the prose sound professionally written in the resolved language, with native idiom and syntax, without importing Swedish phrasing into English or generic translated English into Swedish? Separate this from locale mechanics. | Both |
| L2 | Does the resolved locale govern spelling, punctuation and number/date/currency forms? Established variation is preserved; do not invent a new factual date or currency conversion. | Both, particularly final Proofread |

| R1 | Does Redline address concrete visible defects while preserving working voice, arguments, quotations and claims outside findings? No unavailable-source verification. | Redline only |
| R2 | Does the trace establish full scoped contract loading, fresh correction when needed, budget/re-review and exactly one final installed Proofread pass, with no substantive edit after it? Write loads no review half or peer editorial pass. | Both, respective boundaries |
| O1 | Does the before/after inventory prove the Output Target contract, source preservation and cleanup? An evaluator capture is not a Skill file. No unapproved extra artifacts or surviving scratch. | Both |

Hidden invention in a source-blind control cannot fairly be required of Redline; visible contradictions can.

# Judgement

**R1: PASS. The delivered text is unchanged. G2 fails because the required reader call to action is absent; the reply accurately reports that unresolved finding.** This is a reported remaining quality problem, not an unreported omission.

## 1. Every difference and claim preservation

There are **no differences**: `work/input.md` and `delivered.md` are byte-for-byte identical, including metadata, headings, byline, punctuation and quotations. The text inside the reply's Markdown fence also matches the delivered artifact. Consequently, there are no mechanical corrections, visible-defect repairs, changes of taste or changes to claims to list.

The claim comparison is as follows; every listed assertion retains its original strength, subject, scope, attribution, chronology and modality.

| Location | Input claims compared with delivery | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Metadata and byline | Case study; no technique; British English (`en_GB`); author Thomas Barregren. The author matches the invoking user identified in `criteria.md`. | All unchanged. |
| Headline | Fenwick staff could see which instruments awaited parts. | Unchanged; visibility is not strengthened into faster repairs. |
| Standfirst | The trial summary records 38 jobs in a shared bench schedule; the manager approved continued use for new jobs; the backlog awaited review of status definitions. | All unchanged, including the restriction to new jobs. |
| Lead | Parts-waiting and work-ready jobs appeared on separate paper sheets; Fenwick services brass and woodwind instruments; the team began a six-week Benchline trial in January 2026 after checking status distinction. | All unchanged, including sequence and duration. |
| First section heading and opening paragraph | Benchline configures the workshop's choices; the team defined statuses and update responsibilities; Benchline configured them and trained four staff in one online session; telephone discussions of collection arrangements continued. | All unchanged, including the division of responsibility. |
| First quotation and attribution | Manager Priya Vale answered an email interview on 2 March 2026 about what the team had to settle; agreement on “ready for work” was necessary; a part's presence in the building did not always mean it had reached the right bench. | All unchanged, including “did not always”. |
| Second section heading and opening paragraph | The summary does not measure repair duration; the summary dated 23 February 2026 records 38 jobs and reports visibility of instruments waiting for parts; repair duration, revenue and customer satisfaction were not measured. | All unchanged; neither results nor measurement limits are expanded or suppressed. |
| Backlog paragraph | Vale approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed status definitions. | Unchanged, including the condition on adding the backlog. |
| Final heading, bridge and quotation | Vale reflects on next steps; asked about repeating the choice and changing it, she would use the schedule again for new jobs and allow another week to check status names before adding the backlog. | All unchanged; hypothetical appraisal remains hypothetical. |

**Removal/change reporting:** No claims or other text were removed, changed or added. The reply explicitly reports this and reports it accurately. Legitimate removals: none. Rejected losses: none. The unresolved call to action is assessed below.

## 2. Bridges into quotations

These are the two quotations in input order. Interview circumstances count as the occasion under class (b); they do not by themselves turn an otherwise contextual bridge into class (c).

| Quotation | Input bridge and class | Delivered bridge and class | Change audit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | “Asked in an email interview on 2 March 2026 what the team had to settle, manager Priya Vale wrote:” — **(b)**. “In an email interview on 2 March 2026” names the occasion; “what the team had to settle” names the subject; “manager Priya Vale wrote” supplies attribution. It does not state that the team needed agreement on the meaning of ready for work or that a part could be at the wrong bench. | “Asked in an email interview on 2 March 2026 what the team had to settle, manager Priya Vale wrote:” — **(b)**, for the same words and reasons. | Unchanged. No bridge change needs reporting; no event, fact, name or figure was supplied; no contextual information was lost. |
| 2 | “Asked about making the same choice again and what would change, Vale wrote:” — **(b)**. “Making the same choice again and what would change” names the subjects; “Vale wrote” supplies attribution. It does not give her affirmative answer, the restriction to new jobs or the additional week. | “Asked about making the same choice again and what would change, Vale wrote:” — **(b)**, for the same words and reasons. | Unchanged. No bridge change needs reporting; no event, fact, name or figure was supplied; no contextual information was lost. |

**Earlier overlap, assessed separately from the immediate bridges:**

- Before quotation 1, “The team defined the statuses and decided who would update them” establishes the work already done. The heading “Benchline configures the workshop’s choices” names Benchline's role. Neither has already delivered the quotation's explanation about agreement on readiness or the distinction between building and bench.
- Before quotation 2, both the standfirst and the backlog paragraph describe approval for new jobs and deferred backlog entry pending status review. That repeats the actual decision and overlaps the quotation's subject. The quotation adds a retrospective hypothetical choice and a specific additional week. “Vale reflects on the next steps” names the topic without giving that appraisal. This earlier overlap does not change the immediate bridge's class.

Neither immediate bridge contains a substantive pre-echo clause or an independent story fact beyond subject, occasion and attribution.

## 3. Quotations themselves

1. **Unchanged:** ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’ Wording and punctuation are identical. The necessity of agreement, the qualified “did not always”, meaning, certainty and the speaker's practical explanatory voice survive intact.
2. **Unchanged:** ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’ Wording and punctuation are identical. The favourable appraisal remains restricted to new jobs; both “would” statements remain hypothetical; the additional week and prerequisite check remain intact. Meaning, stance, reservations and first-person voice survive.

There are no quotation changes to disclose. The reply's assertion that the complete text is unchanged accurately covers both quotations.

## 4. Criterion decisions

| Criterion | Decision | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| G1 | **PASS** | The case study has a recognisable angle: visibility of job status. It carries customer situation, action, limited results and appraisal. A reader learns who chose and configured the statuses, what the trial showed, what it did not measure and why backlog adoption was deferred. No separate named readership is supplied. The missing required action is recorded under G2. |
| G2 | **FAIL** | Headline, standalone standfirst, supported byline, lead before the first H2, explanatory sections and appraisal are present. The ending gives Vale's hypothetical next steps, but does not call the reader to action. The reply explicitly identifies this mandatory omission and leaves it unresolved. |
| P1 | **PASS** | The distinction between parts-waiting and work-ready jobs is introduced before its significance is explained. Team decisions, configuration, recorded results, measurement limits and conditional adoption follow coherently. The quotation explains why physical availability alone is insufficient. No conclusion exceeds the visible evidence. |
| W1 | **PASS** | The headline has 8 words and 55 characters. The seven prose paragraphs contain 31, 42, 36, 45, 35, 20 and 35 words; none exceeds 80. Six of seven have two or three sentences. H2 sections have 2, 2 and 1 paragraphs, so most have two or three and none exceeds three. There are no headings below H2. Standfirst and lead open with different words, “Fenwick” and “Jobs”, and perform complementary jobs; the body remains complete without the standfirst. No reader loss from density or fragmentation is evident. |
| L1 | **PASS** | The prose uses professional, idiomatic English and clear syntax. “Awaiting parts”, “ready for work” and “collection arrangements” work naturally in context. No translated phrasing warrants correction. |
| L2 | **PASS** | British single quotation marks, apostrophes and day–month–year dates are consistent with `en_GB`. “23 February 2026” and “2 March 2026” are retained. No visible spelling, punctuation or locale defect requires repair. |
| R1 | **PASS** | The review identifies the visible mandatory ending defect, reports it as unresolved and preserves every claim, quotation, qualification and the working voice. It makes no taste edits and does not misuse individual paragraph or section preferences. Its report of no removals, changes or additions is exact. |

**Irreparable finding within the supplied text:** The case-study call to action remains missing. G2 requires it to be built from supplied offers, links or contact routes, and the input provides none. The reviewer cannot supply those facts from unavailable material. Leaving this for the writer and reporting it is appropriate; reporting does not make the delivered text pass G2.

No other requested criterion is skipped. The reply's statement that measured anatomy limits pass is supported by the counts above; it does not establish that the missing mandatory ending passes. Claims about correction rounds or mechanical-pass execution are not treated as trace evidence. No traces, configuration files, identities or unavailable source material were inspected.
